executive_summary: August 2026 presents a split personality: investors are broadly optimistic about returns over the next year and overwhelmingly confident that any short-term dip will bounce back fast. Yet crash worries have actually intensified, and many still see the market as expensive. It's a bit like fastening your seatbelt while flooring the accelerator — people expect a good ride but acknowledge the road could get rough.

key_findings.headline: Institutions Rebound, Individuals Steady
key_findings.interpretation: After a dip in July, institutional confidence in higher prices a year from now snapped back to its June level of roughly 86%. Individual investors held steady near 72%, suggesting their optimism never wavered much in the first place.

key_findings.headline: Crash Fears Creep Higher
key_findings.interpretation: Only 30% of institutional investors and 22% of individuals feel confident a crash won't happen in the next six months — both readings dropped from July. This may reflect rising geopolitical uncertainty, valuation jitters, or simply the memory of past summer selloffs.

key_findings.headline: Dip-Buying Faith Surges
key_findings.interpretation: Every single institutional respondent — 100% — believes a 3% daily drop would fully recover within two days, and nearly 88% of individuals agree. This is a dramatic jump from July's mid-40s readings, suggesting deep faith in the market's short-term resilience.

key_findings.headline: Valuation Views Diverge Sharply
key_findings.interpretation: Two-thirds of institutional investors say the market is not overvalued, up from 60% in July. But only 40% of individuals share that view, essentially unchanged. Some institutional managers may hold an efficient-markets perspective in which the current price is by definition the right price, making the gap partly philosophical.

detailed_analysis:
The standout number this month is Buy-on-Dips confidence. Jumping from the mid-40s to 100% among institutions and nearly 88% among individuals is remarkable. One reading of this: investors may believe that underlying liquidity and market structure are strong enough to absorb any one-day shock. Another possibility is that recent quick recoveries from minor pullbacks have reinforced a "buy-the-dip" reflex. Either way, conviction here is about as high as the index can go.

Meanwhile, crash worry tells a different story. Crash Confidence fell to 30% for institutions and 22% for individuals — meaning roughly seven out of ten investors on both sides think a crash is at least plausible. This coexists oddly with the dip-buying enthusiasm. It may suggest people distinguish between a garden-variety 3% drop (easily absorbed) and a broader market meltdown (harder to dismiss). In other words, they trust the trampoline for small falls but worry about the cliff.

The 1-Year Outlook remains solidly optimistic, particularly among institutional managers at nearly 86%. This could reflect expectations around corporate earnings, easing monetary policy, or simply trend-following after a strong run. Individual investors, at 72%, are positive but noticeably more cautious — a gap that has persisted for most of the summer.

Valuation confidence is where the institutional-individual divide is sharpest. At 67% versus 40%, professionals are far more comfortable with current prices. Part of this gap may be philosophical: many institutional managers subscribe to some version of market efficiency, in which the question of overvaluation is essentially moot because the price already reflects all available information. For individual investors without that framework, today's prices may simply feel high relative to historical benchmarks. Neither perspective is inherently more correct — they're measuring different things.
methodology: These indices come from the Yale/Shiller U.S. Stock Market Confidence Surveys, which have tracked investor sentiment since 1989. Each month, roughly 100 wealthy individual investors and 100 institutional investment managers answer the same standardized questions. The consistency of those questions over 35+ years is what makes the data meaningful — you can actually compare investor psychology across very different market environments. The four indices each measure something distinct: • 1-Year Confidence: The share who expect prices to be higher in 12 months. • Crash Confidence: The share who believe a crash in the next 6 months is very unlikely (under 10% probability). A low reading means most people think a crash is plausible. • Buy-on-Dips Confidence: The share who believe that after a 3% single-day market drop, prices would fully recover within two days. • Valuation Confidence: The share who do not believe the market is overvalued. Surveys were conducted semi-annually before 2001 and have been monthly since July 2001. Respondents rotate over time, but consistent characteristics — high income, investment experience — are maintained across the panel.
